Text: Legacy `java.util.Date` months are {{c1::0-indexed}} (0 = January), whereas modern `java.time.LocalDate` months are {{c2::1-indexed}} (1 = January).
Extra: In java.util.Date and Calendar, months range from 0 to 11. In the java.time package, they range from 1 to 12.

Text: Legacy `java.util.Date` constructor expects the year argument to be {{c1::year minus 1900}} (e.g., 126 represents the year 2026).
Extra: This subtraction makes legacy Date creation extremely error-prone and hard to read.

Text: SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe because it internally maintains mutable state in a shared {{c1::Calendar}} instance.
Extra: If shared across multiple threads, format() and parse() operations will overwrite each other's data, causing garbage output or exceptions.

Text: Modern Java date-time classes (like `LocalDate`) are {{c1::immutable}} and thread-safe, meaning modification methods return new instances.
Extra: Because they are immutable, they can be shared freely across threads without synchronization, preventing shared state bugs.

Text: LocalDate represents a date without time or timezone, while LocalTime represents time without date or timezone, both formatted using the {{c1::ISO-8601}} calendar system.
Extra: The default format is yyyy-MM-dd for LocalDate and HH:mm:ss for LocalTime.

Text: LocalDateTime combines date and time but lacks a {{c1::timezone offset}}, so it does not represent a unique instant on the global timeline.
Extra: Without an offset or zone, '10:00 AM' represents a different absolute point in time in New York compared to Tokyo.

Text: ZonedDateTime contains a date, time, offset, and a regional {{c1::ZoneId}} (e.g. `America/New_York`) to automatically handle DST rules.
Extra: This class is optimal for user-facing applications that need to dynamically resolve transitions like Daylight Saving Time.

Text: OffsetDateTime contains date, time, and a fixed offset (represented by {{c1::ZoneOffset}}), but does not have regional timezone rules.
Extra: Because it has a fixed offset without DST rules, it is widely used for system integration, databases, and network serializations.

Text: Instant represents a point on the timeline measured in seconds and nanoseconds relative to the {{c1::Unix Epoch}} (January 1, 1970 UTC).
Extra: It acts as a timezone-neutral UTC timestamp. Its toString() representation always appends 'Z'.

Text: Passing LocalDate to `Duration.between()` throws {{c1::UnsupportedTemporalTypeException}} because LocalDate lacks time-based units like seconds.
Extra: Duration only operates on time-based objects (Instant, LocalTime, LocalDateTime). Use Period.between() for date-based objects.

Text: Period represents a date-based amount of time, whereas Duration represents a {{c1::time-based}} amount of time.
Extra: Period is measured in years, months, and days. Duration is measured in seconds and nanoseconds.

Text: Printing a Period displays a string in ISO-8601 format beginning with the prefix {{c1::P}} (e.g. `P1Y2M`).
Extra: For example, P1Y2M3D represents a period of 1 year, 2 months, and 3 days.

Text: Chaining static factories like `Period.ofYears(1).ofDays(5)` produces a period containing only {{c1::5 days}} because the last static call overrides previous values.
Extra: To get a period representing both, use Period.of(1, 0, 5) or use plus methods.

Text: In DateTimeFormatter patterns, uppercase `M` represents {{c1::month}}, whereas lowercase `m` represents {{c1::minute}}.
Extra: Confusing these two is a very common bug, resulting in values like '2026-30-12' where minutes are printed instead of month.

Text: Parsing an invalid date format string throws the runtime exception {{c1::DateTimeParseException}}.
Extra: This occurs when the characters do not match the expected pattern or when required components (like time) are missing.

Text: Comparing two date-times using the `equals()` method checks for exact object equality, whereas {{c1::isEqual()}} compares chronological positions on the timeline.
Extra: For instance, ZonedDateTime at +01:00 vs +02:00 representing the same instant will return true for isEqual() but false for equals().

Text: Complex date adjustments, such as finding the next Tuesday, are performed using the {{c1::TemporalAdjusters}} utility class.
Extra: TemporalAdjusters provides standard adjusters like next(), lastDayOfMonth(), and firstDayOfNextYear().

Text: To adjust a ZonedDateTime to a target timezone while maintaining the exact same global instant, use the {{c1::withZoneSameInstant()}} method.
Extra: In contrast, withZoneSameLocal() retains the local digits, changing the actual moment on the timeline.

Text: During a spring-forward DST transition, adding a {{c1::Period}} preserves local time digits, while adding a {{c2::Duration}} adds exact physical seconds, potentially shifting local time.
Extra: Period is date-based and keeps local digits constant. Duration is time-based and adds exact physical time.

Text: If a local date-time falls in a DST gap, ZonedDateTime adjusts the time {{c1::forward}} by the transition offset; if it falls in an overlap, it uses the {{c2::earlier}} offset by default.
Extra: For gaps, it adjusts forward to a valid time. For overlaps, it defaults to the earlier offset.

Text: DateTimeFormatter is stateless and immutable, meaning all formatting state is kept on the calling thread's {{c1::execution stack}}, avoiding race conditions.
Extra: Statelessness makes it fully thread-safe, unlike SimpleDateFormat which holds state in a shared Calendar.
